data.title: Canada to Pursue Legislation to Revamp Regulatory System
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canada's Liberal government will introduce legislation in the coming weeks that builds upon previous efforts to accelerate the construction of projects and attract private capital.

Senior cabinet minister Dominic LeBlanc said Friday the proposed changes to project reviews will maintain robust environmental protection and respect Ottawa's constitutional responsibility to consult with the country's indigenous communities.

Besides managing a turbulent trade relationship with the U.S., Prime Minister Mark Carney has made the lure of private investment and the construction of infrastructure and resource projects an urgent policy priority. Some of his most notable policy changes to date have focused on establishing more certainty regarding the regulatory-review process.

This week, the government said that proposed oil-and-gas pipelines, natural-gas plants and electricity-transmission lines would no longer be subject to a secondary assessment under a scheme introduced by former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau.

LeBlanc--whose assignment includes addressing investment and growth barriers within Canada--said the energy-related changes "will again bring more coherence and predictability" for investors, he told reporters at a cabinet conference in Banff, Alberta. "The idea was to take a specific narrow group of important projects, and centralize the federal review process in the hands of the people that have the most experience in those particular kinds of projects."

Initial steps to date by the Carney administration have been received positively, particularly resource-rich Alberta, which said regulations introduced by Trudeau led to a stagnation in investment and threatened the province's livelihood. Anger about the regulatory process has partly fueled a nascent independence movement in Alberta, with a vote scheduled for Oct. 19 on whether the province should pursue a referendum on sovereignty.

The C.D. Howe Institute, a Toronto think tank, said the regulatory system requires further thinning. The Carney government has set up a new agency to accelerate the approval of major projects deemed of the national interest, but that "does not resolve underlying problems," the think tank said in an analysis this week.

"None of these mechanisms address the fundamental sources of uncertainty in Canada: political decision-making over individual projects and open-ended criteria that require regulators to consider broad public-policy objectives," the think tank said.

data.title: Tesla could transform the trucking business - and capitalize on high diesel prices
data.description:
By William Gavin

The EV maker aims to finally kick its long-awaited Semi truck into high gear - unlocking a potentially huge opportunity, according to Morgan Stanley

Tesla's all-electric Semi is the company's ticket to becoming a winner in autonomous trucking, analysts say.

Diesel prices have reached a new record, likely making everything from grocery shopping to commuting to work more expensive. But for Tesla, that price spike represents an opportunity.

Tesla (TSLA) is ramping up the Semi - a fully electric, heavy-duty semi truck that was introduced in late 2017 and began rolling off a high-volume production line in April. CEO Elon Musk has also said Tesla will aim to offer self-driving Tesla Semis by 2027.

Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco wrote on Friday that he long believed Tesla was a "potential wildcard in the competitive landscape" of autonomous trucks. Now, the company is becoming a "credible emerging competitor," he said.

Tesla plans to host an inauguration event on Sept. 24 for the Nevada facility that had previously outlined a production target of 50,000 Semis per year. The vehicle has attracted orders from several major companies, including Walmart (WMT), PepsiCo (PEP) and Einride (ENRD), with the latter aiming to deploy 500 Semis.

Autonomous trucking could be a boon for the freight industry, thanks to a combination of lower labor costs and less fuel waste. Diesel costs are on the rise - reaching a new peak of $6 per gallon, on average, in the U.S. this week, according to AAA.

Percoco said that an autonomous fleet could be between six and eight times as profitable as a human-driven fleet. The "most important takeaway" for Tesla investors is what the company can make off its autonomous software, he noted. Tesla sells its Full Self-Driving advanced driver-assistance system to customers as a monthly subscription.

The analyst estimated that Tesla could generate between $12,000 and $18,000 per month for each vehicle, basing that figure off a subscription fee and an assumed amount of miles driven per month. By 2040, that could represent a $17 billion stream of software revenue, Percoco added, assuming that Tesla accounts for 13.5% of the market.

"Tesla Semi represents an underappreciated driver of earnings growth through 2040," he wrote.

Percoco, who is neutral on Tesla's stock, said his expectations for the Semi led him to raise the price target for his Tesla bull case to $840, from $820. His $400 base price target was left untouched.

Tesla's stock inched slightly higher in recent action on Friday, to trade at around $365 a share.

There are a few caveats. In a separate note to clients, Morgan Stanley analyst Ravi Shanker warned that while autonomous trucking is "more real than ever," it's also still just a "promise" until commercial production ramps up in 2027. Most of the vehicles currently on the road, even those generating revenue, are still basically prototypes, he added.

Tesla has also put the Semi's self-driving software on the back burner as it focuses on the newly deployed Cybercab and its other vehicles. Musk told investors in July he doesn't want the Semi to "be a distraction" over the next several months.

Morgan Stanley also sees Aurora Innovation (AUR) and Kodiak AI (KDK) as potential autonomous-trucking winners. The firm expects Aurora to control 22.5% of the autonomous-vehicle market by 2040, while Kodiak would have an estimated 8.8% share.

Shanker raised his price target on Aurora's stock to $18 from $14, and initiated coverage on Kodiak's stock with a $9 price target. Morgan Stanley has a buy rating on Aurora's stock and the equivalent of a neutral rating on Kodiak's.

Aurora shares were up nearly 3% in recent trading on Friday, while Kodiak shares gained more than 3%.

-William Gavin

data.title: I went to a dinner party, brought an appetizer and wine - and the host charged me $60. Should I cut ties with her?
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

'Am I right to think this is pretty cheap and rude?'

"She explained that she was charging everyone who attended because it had been an expensive meal."

Dear Dollar Signs,

I was invited to a dinner party by a new friend. I volunteered to bring a charcuterie board for the group - there were about eight people expected - and I also brought a bottle of wine.

Everything was lovely. She made fish and vegetables and had other sides, including mashed potatoes. A few of the other guests also brought sides and appetizers.

The next day, I sent her a message thanking her for inviting me. She responded with a sweetly worded request for $60. She explained that she was charging everyone who attended because it had been an expensive meal.

I found the whole thing bizarre.

Am I right to think this is pretty cheap and rude? I paid her $60, but now I'm nervous about accepting another invitation from her. Maybe, going forward, I should ask ahead of time whether she'd prefer that I Venmo her money rather than bring a dish or appetizer.

The whole thing feels so odd to me. How should I handle invitations from this person in the future?

Dinner for Schmucks

If you're just starting out on your money or career journey and have questions about how to navigate your finances, we want to hear from you. Write to Dollar Signs, MarketWatch's new advice column, at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

Dear Diner,

Yes, this is bizarre behavior. And the math is suspicious. If all eight guests gave her $60 that means she accumulated $480. Unless this fish was topped with literal caviar, the meal you're describing doesn't sound like it would be near $500, especially if guests were also contributing sides and appetizers. And how much of it did she cover, herself, then?

This woman seems to have a very unorthodox view of hosting - and I wouldn't assume that it's new. If you have a problem with being blindsided by requests for money, I'd cut ties now. If I had to guess, this is very normal to her and will show up in other social scenarios should you continue a relationship.

It's one thing to want your guests to pitch in - it's another to surprise them with a pretty hefty bill after inviting them over for a meal. If you're going to charge a whopping $60 to cook for people, you'd better tell them beforehand.

That being said, I think you did the right thing. Had you written to me before you acquiesced, I would have told you to pay it, but beware of this behavior going forward.

There is also a less costly, more upfront way to host and not spend a ton of money. Recently, a friend had a barbeque and asked everyone to pay her $10, in lieu of bringing a dish. She hosts quite frequently and noticed that there is always a lot of food waste. She told me she'd rather everyone just bring what they want to drink and leave the food menu to her.

It went quite smoothly. I was happy to pay $10 and not risk seeing my bag of chips and jar of salsa sit unopened on the kitchen counter. It was clear why I was paying the money and the disclosure was made up front - not after the fact.

I sense that part of your discomfort with cutting her off is that this is a new friend, and I can empathize. Making friends as an adult can be hard. When you find one that is gracious enough to host you, it can feel like discovering a rare gem in a mine of homebodies and those siloed to their own friend groups or families.

If the relationship is worth saving, I'd maybe take the financial reins. Put any drinks or movie tickets on your card, and then charge her after the fact. This makes it so the total cost of the outing isn't left up to her judgement.

But, if you have a problem with this kind of rigidity around money, I don't think it's going to work out long term. I promise, there are tons of other people whose financial and communication habits align more with your own. Find them. They are probably more fun than someone who spends $500 on a piece of fish for an eight-person dinner party, anyway.

Write to Dollar Signs at dollarsigns@marketwatch.com.

-Aditi Shrikant

data.title: Great Lakes Pickleball Club Celebrates Official Grand Opening in Grand Rapids
data.description:
Great Lakes Pickleball Club Celebrates Official Grand Opening in Grand Rapids

Great Lakes Pickleball Club (GLPC) celebrated its official Grand Opening on Wednesday, September 9, at its Grand Rapids facility, located at 4180 Jupiter Ave NE, Grand Rapids, MI 49525.

The celebration, held from 2:00 - 8:00 PM, welcomed community members, local businesses, partners, and pickleball players of all experience levels. An official ribbon-cutting ceremony took place at 3:30 PM, marking an exciting milestone for the club and its continued growth in the Grand Rapids community.

“Opening Great Lakes Pickleball Club is a momentous event for us. It represents our passion for the sport, but even more importantly, our commitment to building community through competition, health, and wellness. We’re excited to grow this club around those pillars of stewardship and create a place where people of all ages can come together, compete, have fun, and build relationships,” said Brandon Teets, owner and founder of Great Lakes Pickleball Club.

Great Lakes Pickleball Club is more than a place to play; it is a year-round destination for pickleball, recreation, and community in West Michigan. The Grand Rapids facility features four indoor pickleball courts, two golf simulators, lessons and programming for players of all skill levels, leagues, memberships, events, and additional wellness amenities. Whether someone is picking up a paddle for the first time, looking for competitive play, planning a group or corporate event, or simply looking for a place to stay active and connect with others, GLPC is designed to offer something for everyone.

Throughout the event, guests toured the facility, met the GLPC team, experienced the club’s indoor pickleball courts and amenities, and learned more about memberships, leagues, lessons, events, and other opportunities available at the club.

The Grand Opening also featured local vendors, food and drinks, games, activities, raffles, prizes, and opportunities for guests to get on the courts and experience GLPC firsthand.

Local businesses and partners that have supported the club also joined GLPC, including 100GROUP, GLPC’s point-of-sale and payment processing partner. 100GROUP provides payment technology and processing solutions that help support the club’s day-to-day operations.

The event also allowed GLPC to share more about the Michigan High School Pickleball Association (MHSPA), an initiative developed by GLPC to help bring organized pickleball opportunities to Michigan high school students. MHSPA is working to create a structured environment centered around competition, development, leadership, and community while helping grow the sport at the high school level.

“Most importantly, we want to get our youth involved from the very beginning and help introduce the next generation to a sport that can bring a lifetime of competition, friendship, and healthy living,” Teets said. “This is just the beginning of what we believe can become something truly special for our community.”

The Grand Opening marks an important next step for Great Lakes Pickleball Club as it continues to expand its programming, develop community partnerships, and create new opportunities for players of all ages and experience levels to play, compete, and connect.

About Great Lakes Pickleball Club

Great Lakes Pickleball Club is an indoor pickleball facility serving the greater Grand Rapids community. GLPC offers four indoor pickleball courts, two golf simulators, lessons, memberships, and additional wellness amenities designed to create a welcoming environment for both new and experienced players.

data.title: Tenon Medical Announces Warrant Inducement for Aggregate Gross Proceeds of Approximately $2,872,338
data.description:
LOS GATOS, CA / ACCESS Newswire / September 11, 2026 / Tenon Medical, Inc. (NASDAQ:TNON) ("Tenon" or the "Company"), a medical device company dedicated to transforming care for patients with certain sacro-pelvic disorders announced today it has entered into warrant exercise agreements with an institutional investor to exercise outstanding warrants to purchase an aggregate of 572,179 of the Company's shares of common stock (the "Existing Warrants"). In consideration for the immediate exercise in full of the Existing Warrants for gross cash proceeds of $2,872,338.58, the exercising holders will receive in a private placement new unregistered warrants (the "New Warrants") to purchase up to an aggregate of 858,269 shares of common stock (equal to 150% of the shares of common stock issued in connection with the exercise of the Existing Warrants) with an exercise price of $5.02 per share. The New Warrants are immediately exercisable on the date of issuance and will expire five years from the date of issuance.

The closing of the offering is expected to occur on or about September 14, 2026, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. The gross proceeds from the warrant inducement are expected to be $2,872,338.58, excluding any proceeds that may be received upon the exercise of the New Warrants and before deducting financial advisor fees and other expenses payable by the Company.

WallachBeth Capital is acting as financial advisor for the warrant inducement transaction.

The New Warrants described above were offered in a private placement pursuant to an applicable exemption from the registration requirements of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the "Act") and, along with the shares of common stock issuable upon their exercise, have not been registered under the Act, and may not be offered or sold in the United States absent registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission ("SEC") or an applicable exemption from such registration requirements. The Company has agreed to file a registration statement with the SEC covering the resale of the shares of common stock issuable upon exercise of the New Warrants (the "Resale Registration Statement").

This press release does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy, nor will there be any sales of these securities in any jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of such jurisdiction.

About Tenon Medical, Inc.

Tenon Medical, Inc., a medical device company dedicated to transforming care for patients with certain sacro-pelvic disorders. Tenon was incorporated in the State of Delaware in 2012 and currently offers two systems to treat a diseased sacroiliac joint (the "SI Joint"). The Company has developed The Catamaran™ SI Joint Fusion System that offers a novel, less invasive approach to the SI Joint using a single, robust titanium implant. In August 2025, the Company acquired substantially all of the assets of SiVantage, Inc. and SIMPL Medical, LLC, including the SImmetry+® SI Joint Fusion System, which treats disorders of the SI Joint through a minimally invasive lateral access solution that incorporates well-established orthopedic fusion principles. Since the national launch of The Catamaran System in October 2022, Tenon is focused on three commercial opportunities: 1) primary SI Joint procedures, 2) revision procedures of failed SI Joint implants and 3) SI-Joint fusion adjunct to a spine fusion construct.

data.title: Why a shrinking population doesn't have to be the kiss of death for an economy or stock market
data.description:
By Mark Hulbert

Investors are all wrong about demography, a new study finds. Keep that in mind when allocating your portfolio.

I'm taking issue with the widespread belief that the long-term fates of a country's economy and stock market are closely tied to the size of its population. Though demographic determinism has a long history, in recent decades it perhaps has been most widely associated in the investment arena with financial analyst and author Harry Dent.

A new study questions this determinism. Titled "Baby Busts and Growth Booms: Demographic Change and the Macroeconomy," the study began circulating in academic circles this summer. Its authors are Daron Acemoglu, David Autor and Keelan Beirne of MIT and Andrew Scott of the London Business School. The authors found that "lower birth rates are associated with higher growth in GDP per working-age adult" and that these two trends mostly cancel each other out - leaving a country's overall GDP largely unchanged as populations ebb and flow.

This finding may be good news for investors in countries whose populations are set to decline in coming decades. China's population in 2100 is projected to be more than 50% lower than today, for example, with Japan's 40% lower and Brazil's 23% smaller. If demography were destiny, then the long-term prospects of these countries' equities would be dismal.

Though the U.S. population is projected to grow modestly through 2100, the country is projected to fall from third to sixth place in a ranking of the world's most populous countries.

This new study will also be welcome news to investors in U.S. equities. Though the U.S. population is projected to grow modestly through 2100, the country is projected to fall from third to sixth place in a ranking of the world's most populous countries.

The study's authors effectively found that necessity is the mother of invention. When a country has a relative scarcity of younger workers, that country's technology sector rises to the occasion, resulting in "more labor-saving patents and growing high-tech activity." In addition, the authors found that countries with a relative shortage of workers experience faster growth in "Total Factor Productivity," which is the fraction of economic growth that can't be traced back to either labor or capital.

Many investors will react with incredulity, pointing to Japan as Exhibit A of why demography is destiny. The country's population was already plateauing by the late 1980s, when the Nikkei 225 (NIY00) stock average hit a peak that wasn't eclipsed for nearly four decades. The country's population today is lower than where it stood in the late 1980s and is projected to decline by nearly 40% more between now and the end of this century.

A glaring counterexample is South Korea. For many years it has been clear to demographers that its population was about to go over a cliff - yet its stock market has performed admirably. Its population hit a peak in 2020 and is projected to be 58% lower at the end of this century - even a bigger decline in percentage terms than in the case of China. And yet the iShares South Korea ETF EWY has held its own relative to the S&P 500 over the last couple of decades - even before this year, when South Korea's stock market has skyrocketed.

It is possible that other factors account for this new study's findings. Some have suggested that the bearish impact of a declining population can be avoided by an increasing share of women in the workforce and/or an increasingly educated workforce. But the researchers report that they found "little evidence" of support for these alternative explanations.

The investment implication of this new research is that long-term investors need not obsess about demographic projections when picking countries in which to invest. To illustrate, consider the accompanying chart that plots the relationship between the 20 largest developed countries' population growth over the 2000-25 period and the corresponding performance of their stock markets. Notice that the best-fit trend line is sloping slightly downward; though the angle of that slope is not a statistically significant difference from flat, the fact that it is downwardly sloping at all runs counter to what up until now has been the prevailing wisdom that an expanding population is a long-term economic positive.

The table below lists stocks of companies based outside the U.S. that currently are recommended by any of the investment newsletters monitored by my performance auditing firm. You'll notice that many of the companies are from countries with a projected population decline. If you had been avoiding such stocks because of what used to be the conventional wisdom, you can now consider each on its own merits rather than its country's demography - just as the newsletter editors already are doing.

data.title: The traditional paths to building wealth are -2-
data.description:
Members of Gen Z said that on average it takes an annual income of $500,000 to be successful, more than twice the average amount cited by all respondents. Many want to retire earlier than previous generations did.

Faced with economic uncertainty, about 43% of Gen Z-ers now have a side hustle, according to a 2026 LendingTree survey. More than half of them see these gigs as supporting their long-term financial security, and 35% plan to continue with them until their main job provides more income.

In response to high costs, more working young adults are living with their parents.

A growing number are also focusing on how they can thrive when companies reward owners and shareholders more than workers. Labor compensation as a share of non-farm GDP fell to 52.9% in the second quarter this year, "the lowest level in the series which begins in the first quarter of 1947," according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

One result of this shift in awareness has been a sixfold increase in investing by younger people since 2015, catalyzed by technology that has made the stock market more accessible. In 2024, 37% of 25-year-olds had moved money into investment accounts since age 22, up from 6% in 2015, according to the JPMorganChase Institute.

Even so, many young workers are not yet participating in the stock market. Some don't know how to, and others cannot afford to.

Still, "it's never been more obvious that wealth begets wealth," economic commentator Kyla Scanlon, who is herself a member of Gen Z, recently wrote, noting that since 1990, median pay has increased by 18%, home prices by 66%, and S&P 500 SPX returns by 1,500%. "Wealth - ownership - feels like it matters more than any sort of labor income, because wealth builds more wealth."

Nicole Ingham, at 33 a young millennial or "zillennial," said her parents always taught her to save money, but never taught her about investing.

Her parents, who were in the military, "were able to get to financial prosperity through hard work and grit and determination," she said. "I want ease, and I want space, and I want time. And those are things my parents never had." Because she didn't have the job security or pension that comes with a military career, she worried that simply working and saving would tether her to "the middle-class trap: working until 65 and still not able to retire," she said.

After being exposed to investing through a job at a financial-technology company, Ingham said she "became pretty obsessed with the idea of buying my life back." She started investing most of her salary while she and her husband lived off his $65,000 income, the larger of the two.

Their investable net worth now is just over $1 million, which is in sector-based and total-market index funds as well as individual stocks. This has allowed Ingham to step away from her corporate job and start her own business as a financial coach in Jacksonville, Fla. She plans to hire their two children to do work for her company to jump-start their ability to build wealth, with the aim of setting them up to be multimillionaires by the time they retire.

"As soon as you figure it out, it's like the secret is out, and you're like, 'Oh, there's another way,'" Ingham said.

Kaylee Archibald, age 31, said she has been able to invest about 25% to 30% of her gross income by advocating for higher pay at her job and doing odd jobs such as reselling clothing and pet sitting. "I was lucky enough to have a couple of really great co-workers that pushed me to ask for more [pay]" at work, she told MarketWatch. She mostly invests in index funds such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF VOO, Invesco QQQ Trust QQQ and Vanguard Morningstar Total Stock Market ETF VTI.

"I'm hoping if I stay on track that I'll be work-optional in 10 years," Archibald said. Her father thinks that is "unfathomable," but she believes that by "being intentional now, and investing and saving aggressively, it will change my life."

Outcomes like these, however, are rare. The problem, even for motivated investors, is that for the many people who cannot afford to save aggressively, "steadily investing money into a diversified basket of stocks is a wonderful way to save for your retirement, but it is not a guarantee for getting ahead," said Moore.

Others are exploring entrepreneurship. More than half of Gen Z-ers said they have seriously considered starting a business in the last 12 months, nearly twice the rate of all respondents in a recent poll.

While nearly half of small businesses fail within five years, Kyla Scanlon noted that ownership also affords greater opportunity.

For Will Freeman, age 29, getting ahead meant starting his own consulting firm while working full time. He left his job in 2024, sold his company in 2025 and now works part time as a chief information officer in Tampa.

"I make three times as much as I did at my corporate job and work half the amount of time," he told MarketWatch. While many of his friends went back to school for their MBAs with the goal of working at big consulting firms, he said, "I was already progressing in my career enough, and I didn't have that barrier to getting promoted or creating opportunities for myself."

Many Gen Z-ers say they expect their financial situation to improve over the next year, and about 42% expect to do better than their parents, according to an Urban Institute survey.

Yet many no longer see the old playbook as enough to get ahead. As the paths to prosperity change, Nicole Ingham, the zillennial financial coach, said, "all Americans should have the right to be educated on how to benefit from the growth of the U.S. economy."
